scenarios.scenario: Pitching a new idea to your manager
scenarios.context: An employee proposes a four-day working week trial to her manager.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I'd like to propose a three-month trial of a four-day working week for our team.
Several companies that tried it reported higher productivity, because people were more focused and took fewer sick days.
That's a fair point, which is why I'd suggest staggering the days off so the office is always covered.
We'd measure it carefully. If targets weren't met after three months, we'd return to the old schedule at no cost to the company.
Yes, the idea is the same pay for the same results. Not only would it attract new talent, but it would also keep our current staff motivated.
I'll prepare a one-page summary with the figures and the evaluation plan by Friday.

speakerB.en: That's an ambitious suggestion. What makes you think it would work here?
Those were mostly small firms. Our clients expect us to be available five days a week.
And what if output drops? I can't justify a trial that costs us money.
That reduces the risk considerably. Would the salary stay the same?
I'm not fully convinced, but I'm willing to take it to the directors if you put it in writing.
Good. A clear plan will make it much harder for them to say no.

scenarios.scenario: Answering difficult questions after a talk
scenarios.context: A researcher takes questions from the audience after presenting her findings.

speakerA.en: Thank you for an interesting talk. Your sample was only eighty people. Can you really draw such firm conclusions from it?
Did you consider that the participants were all university students? They might not represent the wider population.
So how confident are you that the effect is real?
I'm not sure I follow your second graph. Could you explain the vertical axis again?
What practical difference would this make for teachers?
Thank you. That was a clear and honest answer.

speakerB.en: A fair challenge. The sample is small, so I'd describe the results as indicative rather than conclusive, and I'd like to repeat the study with more participants.
Yes, and I mention that as a limitation in the paper. Had resources allowed it, I would have recruited from a broader range of ages.
Reasonably confident, since three separate tests pointed the same way, but I wouldn't claim certainty until others replicate it.
Of course. It shows the average improvement in percentage points, so the taller the bar, the greater the benefit.
If the results hold, teachers could adopt the method at almost no cost, which is why I think it's worth investigating further.
Thank you for the questions. They've given me several ideas for the next stage of the research.

scenarios.scenario: Responding to criticism of your proposal
scenarios.context: Two members of a design team discuss feedback on a written proposal.

speakerA.en: I read your proposal, and I think the idea is promising, but the budget section worries me. It seems very optimistic.
The marketing costs. You've assumed they'll stay the same, even though your plan doubles the number of customers.
I'd also suggest including a worst-case scenario, so that readers see you've considered the risks.
On the contrary, it shows you've been realistic, which makes the rest of your argument more credible.
Most people feel like that at first. The trick is to separate the idea from your ego.
Gladly. Send it over when it's ready, and I'll give you my comments within two days.

speakerB.en: I can see why you say that. Which figures in particular do you find unrealistic?
You're right. I hadn't taken that into account. I'll recalculate them using last year's actual figures.
I wouldn't want the proposal to sound negative, though. Won't that weaken the overall message?
That's a good point. I'd been treating criticism as a threat, when it's really a way of improving the idea.
Easier said than done, but I'll try. Would you be willing to read the revised version?
Thanks. Had you not read it first, I would have submitted a much weaker proposal.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a committee to fund a project
scenarios.context: A student society presents a funding request to a university committee.

speakerA.en: Thank you for coming. Please tell us why the society deserves funding, and how much you are requesting.
There are already online courses available for free. What would your workshops offer that they don't?
That's a reasonable argument, but how can we be sure that students will actually attend?
Impressive. What would happen if you received only half of the amount?
And how would you measure the success of the project?
That sounds well thought out. We'll discuss your application and let you know by the end of next week.

speakerB.en: We're requesting 2,000 to run a series of free coding workshops for students from every faculty.
Face-to-face support. Many beginners give up online because nobody is there to help when they get stuck.
Our pilot session last term attracted sixty participants, and over ninety per cent said they would come again.
We'd run fewer workshops and drop the printed materials, but the core programme would still go ahead.
Through attendance figures and a short survey at the end of each session, and we'd report the results to this committee.
Thank you for your time. We're confident that the benefits will far outweigh the cost.

scenarios.scenario: Arguing the opposite side in a debate
scenarios.context: Two members of a debating club prepare for a motion they were assigned to argue.

speakerA.en: I've been assigned the side that says homework should be abolished, but I personally disagree. How do I argue convincingly?
I suppose I could mention research showing that too much homework causes stress, especially for younger pupils.
They'll say homework teaches responsibility and self-discipline. How should I respond?
That's clever. Is it acceptable to concede a point, or does that make me look weak?
I'll try that. What about my tone? I tend to sound too aggressive when I'm nervous.
Thanks. Whether or not I win, arguing the opposite side has already changed how I see the issue.

speakerB.en: Start by finding the strongest evidence for that position, rather than attacking it. You need to understand it from the inside.
Good. Then anticipate the opposition's best objection and answer it before they raise it.
You could argue that those skills can also be developed through projects in class, so homework isn't the only way.
Conceding a minor point actually strengthens your credibility, provided you immediately explain why the main argument still stands.
Slow down and speak calmly. Persuasion works better when the audience feels respected, not attacked.
That's the real value of debating. You learn that few questions have only one reasonable answer.
